analysis.one_liner: Gives Senate candidates the option of public campaign funding in exchange for small-dollar-only fundraising.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the Fair Elections Now Act: it sat in the Rules Committee with 16 of 100 senators cosponsoring, and only one subcommittee hearing was ever held.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Elections Now Act would have created a voluntary system where Senate candidates who collect enough small contributions from in-state residents receive public funding instead of relying on large private donations. Participants would get a base grant, a five-fold match on small-dollar contributions, and broadcast advertising vouchers, and in exchange they could accept only small contributions and spend none of their own wealth. The fund would be financed by a small fee on companies holding large federal contracts, and broadcasters would have to give participating candidates discounted ad rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without access to wealthy donor networks, who could run viable Senate campaigns on small contributions plus public funds; voters, whose senators would no longer depend on large checks from industries regulated by Congress; and small-dollar donors, whose contributions would be matched five-to-one.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Underfunded candidates and ordinary small donors

how_it_helps.text: A candidate who collects thousands of small qualifying contributions from in-state residents becomes eligible for a public allocation of at least $750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district for the general election.
Participating candidates receive a payment equal to 500 percent of each qualified small-dollar contribution they raise.
Participants may accept only small contributions (qualifying contributions of $100 or less from state residents, plus small-dollar gifts) and may not spend personal or family wealth on the campaign.
Participating candidates get broadcast advertising vouchers worth $100,000 per congressional district, plus a cap on television ad rates at 80 percent of the lowest unit charge.
The Fair Elections Fund would be financed in part by a 0.5 percent fee on federal contracts over $10 million, capped at $500,000 per company per year.
Participants must take part in public debates, and the bill tightens disclosure by requiring electronic filing of campaign reports within 24 hours.

analysis.who_pays: Large federal contractors would pay the financing fee; broadcasters would earn less from campaign-season ads under the rate caps and reporting rules; and taxpayers generally would cover any fund shortfall beyond the fee revenue.

drawbacks.text: The fund's main financing mechanism is only a nonbinding 'sense of the Senate' recommending the contractor fee, so the program's funding would depend on future appropriations that Congress could decline to make.

Participation is voluntary and the spending limits apply only to participating candidates, so after the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision (2010) unbound outside groups and wealthy self-funding opponents could still spend without limit against a publicly financed candidate.
The 0.5 percent fee on large federal contracts is a real cost that contractors could pass into their bids, raising the price the government pays.

The bill creates a new five-member Fair Elections Oversight Board inside the FEC and an elaborate matching-payment, voucher, and audit system, adding administrative machinery that would need to work correctly in its first election cycles.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: candidates trade dependence on large donors for public money and small-dollar matching, which would change who senators answer to. The design weaknesses an honest supporter had to acknowledge were funding uncertainty (the financing mechanism was nonbinding), the mismatch between capped candidate spending and unlimited outside spending after Citizens United, and a new administrative apparatus. Those are significant, but they are design problems rather than reasons the bill disappeared: it never received a committee vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on introduction, got one subcommittee hearing, and was never reported out or voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the bill on April 6, 2011, with 12 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
On April 12, 2011, the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution held a hearing on the measure — the only hearing in the action history.
The bill accumulated 16 cosponsors: 15 Democrats and 1 Independent. No Republican cosponsored.
No further action was taken — no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing private campaign-finance system stayed in place: large donors, federal contractors, and broadcast stations kept the status quo, and senators continued raising money under the old rules. Even the bill's backers gained only a hearing, not a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large donors and incumbents relying on them

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: Senate Majority Assistant/Deputy leader; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 12 original cosponsors; delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Good-government and reform groups (the Fair Elections Now coalition)
for.what_they_did: Ran a sustained public campaign for Fair Elections-style public financing of congressional campaigns.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote or reported it out; it received no action after referral.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican signed on as a cosponsor over the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independents; no Republican ever signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where positions could be tested.

industries.note: Companies holding federal contracts over $10 million would pay a 0.5 percent fee (capped at $500,000 per year) to finance the Fair Elections Fund — a funding source deliberately drawn from firms already benefiting from government business. Avoiding the fee means the public-financing program goes unfunded.

Stations would have to sell ad time to participating candidates at no more than 80 percent of the lowest unit charge, could not preempt paid candidate ads, would face possible license revocation for denying candidates access, and would file standardized reports on political ad purchases. Campaign-season advertising is a major revenue source for local broadcasters.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and joint fundraising operations
industries.note: Participating candidates could accept only small contributions and would be barred from joint fundraising committees with any committee other than another candidate's own committee, cutting off the big-check channel that dominates Senate fundraising.

The bill creates an exception letting party committees spend in coordination with participating candidates through funds fed by $500 contributions, and lets candidates exchange ad vouchers with their party. Parties gain a larger role in campaigns that opt into public financing.
